lead: A reinforced concrete beam works only if steel and concrete move together. Bond is the shear stress at their interface that transfers force from concrete to a bar. Without bond the bar would slide out and the section would fail before the steel yields. Development length L_d is the embedded length needed to build up the bar force safely. Designers check it at supports, at curtailment points and wherever a bar must carry its full tension. This chapter covers bond stress, IS 456 development length, anchorage and the support check.
prereq: You need: shear at supports from Chapter 3.1 and Chapter 3.2; partial safety factors from Unit 1; bar stress from Unit 2.

sections.h3: What bond is and why bars are anchored

blocks.text: Bond is the shear stress transferred across the steel–concrete interface. When a bar is pulled, the concrete grips its surface and the force travels from steel into concrete over a length. Two names are used. Flexural bond is the change of bar force along a beam because the bending moment changes. Anchorage bond is the transfer at an end, where a bar must be held so it does not pull out. Both are the same physical action.

items: Adhesion: chemical grip between concrete and steel.
Friction: resistance to sliding along the bar surface.
Mechanical interlock: ribs on deformed bars bear against concrete.

blocks.text: Deformed bars rely mostly on interlock. Plain bars rely on adhesion and friction, so they need hooks or bends. Average bond stress over an embedded length L is τ_bd = F/(π φ L). F is the bar force in N, φ is the bar diameter in mm, L is the embedment in mm, and τ_bd is the bond stress in N/mm². Real bond stress is not uniform: it is high near a crack and low elsewhere. IS 456 uses an average design bond stress that depends on concrete grade and bar surface. For M25 concrete, IS 456 gives τ_bd = 1.4 N/mm² for plain bars in tension. For deformed bars in tension the value is 1.6 times larger: τ_bd = 1.4 × 1.6 = 2.24 N/mm².

Bond failure can be pull-out, where the bar slides, or splitting, where the concrete splits along the bar because cover is small. Splitting is why cover, spacing and transverse steel matter. A bar near a surface has less concrete to confine it. Some syllabi call this topic bond failure and strength.

At ultimate, the force in a tension bar is F = σ_s π φ²/4, where σ_s is the bar stress and φ is the diameter. Put this into the bond equation over the development length L_d: τ_bd = (σ_s π φ²/4)/(π φ L_d). Cancel π and one φ: τ_bd = σ_s φ/(4 L_d). Rearrange:

blocks.where: L<sub>d</sub> is the development length in mm; φ is the bar diameter in mm; σ<sub>s</sub> is the bar stress to develop in N/mm², taken as 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> in tension; τ<sub>bd</sub> is the design bond stress in N/mm²; f<sub>y</sub> is the characteristic yield strength of steel in N/mm².

blocks.text: The factor 0.87 is the code's ultimate steel stress for a tension bar. For Fe415 steel, σ_s = 0.87 × 415 = 361.05 N/mm². A smaller bar gives a smaller L_d because L_d is directly proportional to φ. Four 10 mm bars have total area 4 × 78.54 = 314.16 mm², equal to one 20 mm bar, and their total perimeter is 4 × π × 10 = 125.7 mm versus π × 20 = 62.8 mm for the single 20 mm bar. So the group develops in a shorter length. Deformed bars have a higher τ_bd than plain bars, so their L_d is shorter.

items: Choose the bar diameter φ, steel grade f_y and concrete grade.
Read the design bond stress τ_bd for that concrete grade and bar type.
Compute σ_s = 0.87 f_y for a tension bar.
Compute L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd) in mm. Round upward for detailing.
Check that the available embedment on the correct side of the critical section is at least L_d.

sections.h3: Anchorage at supports and curtailment points

blocks.text: At a simple support the bending moment is near zero, but the bar still carries force from the adjacent span. IS 456 limits the bar diameter so that L_d does not exceed M1/V + L0. M1 is the moment of resistance of the section at the support in N·mm, V is the shear at that section in N, and L0 is the anchorage length beyond the face of the support in mm. The term M1/V is the distance over which the bar force can be built up by the moment gradient. L0 is the physical length inside the support. Use the same units throughout.

At least one-third of the total tension steel required for positive moment at midspan should extend into the support. This keeps the support section tough and provides anchorage. A standard hook or bend gives extra anchorage by bearing and friction. IS 456 allows a hook to count for plain bars; for deformed bars, the straight length is usually enough. Do not add a hook to L_d unless the code permits it.

At a curtailment point, a bar that is no longer needed for bending must still be developed. Extend the bar beyond the theoretical cut-off by L_d. Without this extension the bar can slip at the section where it is still stressed. Curtailment rules and lap splices are covered in Chapter 3.6. Buildable anchorage details are in Chapter 3.7.

Typical checks are beam bottom bars entering a column, slab bars at a support, and footing starter bars. In each case the question is the same: is there enough embedded length on the tension side of the critical section to develop the bar force without pull-out or splitting?

figure.caption: The straight line is the development length for Fe415 deformed bars in M25 concrete. The marked point is the 16 mm bar from the example, with L_d about 645 mm.

spec.aria: Development length rises linearly with bar diameter; the 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25 concrete needs about 645 mm.

examples.question: Find the development length of a 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25 concrete in tension. Take τ_bd = 2.24 N/mm² and σ_s = 0.87 f_y. State the check needed at a simple support.
steps: Data: φ = 16 mm, f_y = 415 N/mm², τ_bd = 2.24 N/mm².
Support check: L_d ≤ M1/V + L0, and at least one-third of the midspan positive moment steel must extend into the support.
examples.answer: L_d ≈ 644.7 mm (0.645 m), and this length must satisfy L_d ≤ M1/V + L0 at the simple support.
examples.check:
fy = 415.0
phi = 16.0
tau = 2.24
sigma = 0.87 * fy
Ld = phi * sigma / (4.0 * tau)
print(round(sigma, 2))
print(round(Ld, 1))

traps: Using f_y instead of 0.87 f_y in L_d. The code stress at ultimate is 0.87 f_y in tension.
Using the bond stress for plain bars with deformed bars, or the reverse. Deformed bars have higher τ_bd and shorter L_d.
Forgetting that L_d must be available on the correct side of the critical section, not just somewhere near the support.
Treating the support width as L_d. The simple-support check uses M1/V + L0, not support width alone.
Confusing development length with lap length. A lap splice transfers force between two bars and is covered in Chapter 3.6.

quiz.a: The embedded length of a bar needed to develop its design force without pull-out.

quiz.q: What is the IS 456 design bond stress for M25 concrete and deformed bars in tension?
quiz.a: 2.24 N/mm² (1.4 × 1.6 for deformed bars in tension).

quiz.q: Why do deformed bars need a shorter development length than plain bars?
quiz.a: Ribs create mechanical interlock, which raises the design bond stress. L_d is inversely proportional to τ_bd, so a higher τ_bd gives a shorter L_d.

quiz.q: Find L_d for a 20 mm Fe500 deformed bar in M30 concrete in tension. Take τ_bd = 2.4 N/mm² and σ_s = 0.87 f_y.
A 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25 concrete has L_d ≈ 645 mm but only 500 mm of embedment is available before a critical section. Name two code-compliant ways to fix the anchorage.
quiz.a: Use a smaller bar diameter because L_d ∝ φ, or increase the concrete grade to raise τ_bd. Using more bars of smaller size also helps.

quiz.q: A 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25 concrete has L_d ≈ 645 mm but the support is only 300 mm wide. Does this prove the anchorage is unsafe?
quiz.a: No. The support check uses L_d ≤ M1/V + L0, not support width alone. L0 is the available embedment, and M1/V accounts for force built up by the moment gradient. Bars can also extend past the support.

quiz.q: Why is splitting more likely with one large bar than with several small bars of the same total area?
quiz.a: The total force is the same, but one large bar concentrates the rib bearing force and has less perimeter per unit area. Several small bars distribute the force and give more confinement, so splitting is less likely.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses bond-slip models and finite element analysis to study anchorage in complex joints. Fibre-reinforced polymer bars need their own development length rules because their surface and stiffness differ from steel. Strut-and-tie models are used for anchorage in deep beams and pile caps.
